summary: For children aged 10-11 (UK Year 6) learning to construct 2-D shapes to a specification with a ruler and protractor: a triangle from a base and the two angles at its ends (Angle-Side-Angle), a triangle from two sides and an included angle (Side-Angle-Side), a rectangle from length and width, or a regular polygon from side length and turn angle. This is a precision procedural skill layered on angle measuring. The accuracy of the finished figure is itself the evidence: measuring its sides and angles against the specification (and, for rectangles and regular polygons, checking whether it closes) exposes whether the sub-skills are secure; an ASA or SAS triangle will close even when it is inaccurate, so closure alone proves little there. There are three dominant, well-documented failure points — two protractor-specific plus one ruler habit: reading the wrong scale on a dual-scale protractor (so the supplement is drawn, e.g. 140° for 40°), and misplacing the protractor (centre off the vertex, zero-line off the drawn side); and, separately, measuring length from the ruler's physical end rather than its zero mark. The remedy taught here is a disciplined, rehearsed routine: estimate the angle first to choose the right scale, centre-on-vertex with zero-line-on-line, ruler zero on the endpoint, then check the finished figure by measuring its sides and angles (and closure, for rectangles and polygons).
misconceptions: Reads the wrong scale on the dual-scale protractor, drawing the supplement (e.g. 60° instead of 120°)
Places the protractor's centre off the vertex or its zero-line off the side, so every angle is a few degrees out or the ray does not start at the vertex
Measures length from the physical end of the ruler rather than the zero mark, adding the end-margin to each length
Treats a 'nearly closing' triangle as correct rather than a signal of accumulated error
Draws sides to look right rather than to the measured length, or turns an inconsistent amount at each corner of a regular polygon

activities.title: Construct a triangle from a base and two base angles (ASA-style)
steps: Rule a base exactly 7 cm long, placing the ruler's zero mark (not its physical end) on the starting point, then mark and join.
At the left endpoint, before reading, decide: is the 40° angle smaller or bigger than a square corner (right angle)? Use that estimate to pick which of the two protractor scale numbers to read.
Place the protractor with its centre hole on the vertex dot and its zero-line exactly along the base, count up from the 0 on the arm laid along the base, mark 40°, and rule the ray.
Repeat at the right endpoint to set a 65° angle and rule the second ray so the two rays meet.

Check the triangle against the specification: re-measure the 40° and 65° angles and the 7 cm base, then measure the third angle, which should be about 75° (the angles of a triangle add up to 180°). If an angle is out by more than about 2°, or the two rays spread apart and never meet (a sign that a supplement such as 140° was drawn), find where the placement or scale error crept in.
activities.insight: The two scales of a dual-scale protractor offer supplementary numbers (e.g. 40 and 140); your own estimate of whether the angle is bigger or smaller than a right angle is what picks the correct one. Careful placement and measuring from zero are what make the figure match its specification. (A base with an angle set at each of its two ends is an angle-side-angle construction.)

activities.title: Isolate placement with a single-scale or numberless protractor
steps: Using a numberless or single-scale protractor, practise seating it: centre hole on the vertex dot, zero-line exactly along the existing side, every time.
Measure and draw several given angles, focusing only on placement while the scale-reading ambiguity is removed.
Once placement is automatic, return to a dual-scale protractor and reintroduce the estimate-first scale choice.
activities.insight: Separating the placement sub-skill from the scale-reading sub-skill lets each become secure before they must be coordinated.

activities.title: Construct a regular polygon by repeating an equal side and an equal turn
steps: Draw a regular pentagon with sides of 4 cm by ruling an equal side, then setting an equal turn at each corner, and repeating.

Use the same angle at every corner: for a regular pentagon each interior angle is 108° (equivalently an exterior turn of 72°, since 360° ÷ 5 = 72°); with a protractor, measure 108° inside the shape from the side just drawn. The side length (4 cm) does not change these angles.
After drawing, check that all five sides are equal in length and all corners turn by the same amount, and that the figure closes back to the start.
activities.insight: A regular polygon is built from a repeated equal side and an equal turn; keeping both consistent is what makes it regular and makes it close.

activities.title: Knowledge check on scale choice and placement (supporting check)
steps: Given an angle, state which of the two protractor scale readings is correct and why (estimate against a right angle first).
Spot a misplaced protractor in a picture (centre off the vertex, or zero-line off the side) and say what is wrong.
Estimate an unlabelled angle as bigger or smaller than a right angle before any reading is given.
activities.insight: The decisions behind a correct construction — scale choice and correct placement — can be reasoned about explicitly, which supports but does not replace actual drawing.

checkQuestion: Put a ruler and a protractor in front of the child. Say: 'Draw a triangle with a base of 7 cm, an angle of 40° at the left end of the base and an angle of 65° at the right end. Then draw a regular pentagon with sides of 4 cm.' Watch how they place the protractor, which scale they read, where they start the ruler, and whether the triangle closes — do not talk them through it.
checkAnswer: Lays the ruler's zero (not its end) on the start point and rules a 7 cm base; places the protractor centre on each base endpoint with the zero-line along the base, reads the correct scale to mark 40° and 65°, and rules the two rays to meet, producing a closed triangle accurate to about ±2° / ±2 mm; constructs the pentagon with equal 4 cm sides and an equal turn at each corner.
